The high surface-area-to-volume ratio of these fish necessitates frequent foraging to meet daily energetic costs, and their short generation time reflects an evolutionary trade-off favoring early and prolific reproduction over extended somatic persistence.

This early maturation strategy is likely an adaptation to high adult mortality rates in dynamic estuarine environments, ensuring that at least some individuals reproduce before succumbing to predation or seasonal habitat degradation. The length-based puberty threshold aligns well with records from other gobiid species inhabiting comparable tropical tidal zones, where small body size and early reproduction constitute a common life-history syndrome. It is noteworthy that despite their small size at puberty, these fish continue to invest in somatic growth, eventually reaching the considerably larger asymptotic dimensions characteristic of older, iteroparous adults.

Although the GSI is determined from gravid individuals, it likely underestimates cumulative lifetime reproductive effort given that this species is capable of multiple spawning events within a single breeding season. The compressed life schedule of this goby culminates in a natural lifespan of approximately 160 days [am = approximately 160 days] at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], a duration that encompasses multiple reproductive bouts for most individuals. Given that the age at birth is a mere 2 days [ab = 2 days] under these thermal conditions, the post-embryonic period available for growth and reproduction spans roughly 158 days at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This rapid turnover is typical of small marine teleosts in warm, productive environments where seasonal windows of opportunity for larval survival are narrow and unpredictable. Comparative data from related gobiids suggest that variation in lifespan is closely tied to ambient temperature, with cooler regimes prolonging development and extending longevity. Field mark-recapture studies are needed to confirm whether senescence occurs abruptly after the final spawning event or whether a gradual post-reproductive decline is evident. Understanding these demographic details is crucial for predicting population resilience in the face of ongoing climate-driven warming of coastal waters.

The ecological role of Psammogobius biocellatus within estuarine food webs is that of an abundant benthic forager, consuming small crustaceans, polychaetes, and detrital matter, thereby linking primary production to higher trophic levels. As a prey item for piscivorous fish and wading birds, its rapid maturation and elevated fecundity per spawning event, which may involve multiple batches over consecutive weeks, ensure demographic persistence despite considerable predation pressure. Fluctuations in water temperature and salinity within mangrove creeks directly influence embryonic duration, larval survival, and the timing of first reproduction, all of which converge to shape the species' characteristically brief lifespan.
